metaDesc: A beach-by-beach guide to Koh Samet, Thailand: Sai Kaew, Ao Phrao, Ao Wong Duean, Ao Thian, plus quiet bays like Ao Kiu and Ao Wai. Honest picks for who each suits, plus how to get there, boat fares and the island entry fee.

h1:
Koh Samet Beaches
Which One to Pick
intro: Koh Samet has a dozen beaches to choose from, and each one has a completely different mood. Some are lively with fire shows all night; others are so quiet you hear nothing but the waves. Pick the wrong beach when you book your room and the whole trip can feel off. We've lined up the main beaches side by side and given you a straight answer on who each one suits.
chips: 🤫 Quiet corners away from the crowds

blocks.html: Koh Samet sits within Khao Laem Ya–Mu Ko Samet National Park in Rayong province. It's only about a 30-minute boat ride from Ban Phe pier. Most of the beaches cluster along the east side of the island, facing the sunrise, while the west side has just one beach where you can watch the sunset over the sea: Ao Phrao. The island isn't big, so you can walk or hop a songthaew between beaches easily, which makes it a good place to base yourself on one beach and wander over to the next.

blocks.text: The main beaches of Koh Samet — compared one by one

items.name: Sai Kaew Beach
items.blurb: The biggest and liveliest beach on the island, at the far north and a short walk from the entrance pier. The sand is fine and white, easy on bare feet, with plenty of watersports by day and beach bars and fire shows running late into the night. Great if you want some buzz, but if you'd rather sleep in peace, pick a spot toward the far end of the beach.
items.meta: Main beach · lively · easiest to reach from the pier

items.name: Ao Wong Duean
items.blurb: Named for its crescent-moon curve, this is the second busiest beach after Sai Kaew but smaller. The shore slopes gently into shallow water that's easy for swimming, and you'll find restaurants, places to stay and convenience stores all in one bay. Speedboats can run straight in here, so it suits anyone who wants both convenience and a nicely balanced atmosphere.
items.meta: Crescent-moon bay · everything in one spot

items.name: Ao Phrao
items.blurb: The island's only west-facing beach, which makes it the one place you can watch the sun set into the sea. The water is clear and the mood calm and private, with upmarket resorts and a beachfront cafe where you can sip a drink and take in the view. It's well away from the bustle of the east side, so it suits couples or anyone who wants a real rest, though room rates run higher than other beaches.
items.meta: West side · sunset views · quiet and calm

items.name: Ao Thian (Candlelight Beach)
items.blurb: Just south of Ao Wong Duean, its name comes from the candlelight the beachside spots used in the old days. The beach is a good length, the water clear, and there are noticeably fewer people than the beaches up north. It faces the sunrise, so wake up early and you can catch the first light from the sand. Good for anyone who wants a pretty beach without the crowds, and it's a short walk back to Ao Wong Duean for food.
items.meta: Next to Ao Wong Duean · quieter · sunrise views

blocks.title: How to choose a beach without regrets
blocks.html: The simple rule: the east side (Sai Kaew, Wong Duean, Thian) is for sunrises, and the west side (Ao Phrao) is for sunsets. If you're coming for just one night and want easy access, go with Sai Kaew or Wong Duean. If you're set on really unwinding, pick a beach further down toward the south for more quiet.

blocks.text: Quiet corners, away from the crowds

blocks.html: If your real goal is to escape the bustle, look at the beaches deeper toward the south and the tip of the island. Fewer people, fewer shops, but in return you get calm and clear water that plenty of visitors say is even prettier than the beaches up north.

items.name: Ao Kiu
items.blurb: Near the tip of the island with just one place to stay, so it's very quiet and private. The draw is a narrow headland where you can see both the sunrise and sunset from one spot.

items.name: Ao Wai
items.blurb: A small, quiet beach in the south with clear water and few people, and no party scene. Ideal if you just want to fall asleep to the sound of the waves.

items.name: Ao Phai / Ao Thap Thim
items.blurb: Just below Sai Kaew, a touch quieter but still an easy walk back to the lively zone. Good for anyone who wants the middle ground between convenient and peaceful.

blocks.text: How to get to Koh Samet + costs

blocks.html: You start at Ban Phe pier in Mueang Rayong district, about a 3-hour drive from Bangkok, or take a minivan or coach to Ban Phe and catch the boat from there. The pier has both regular passenger ferries and speedboats to choose from.

items: Regular passenger ferry — around ฿70/person/trip, taking about 30 minutes. Most dock at the entrance pier (near Sai Kaew Beach), where you can pick up a songthaew to other beaches.
Speedboat — from around ฿200/person/trip, faster at about 10–15 minutes, and runs straight to the beach you've booked, such as Ao Wong Duean or Ao Phrao.
Island entry fee (national park) — around ฿40/person for Thais and ฿200/person for foreigners, paid on arrival.
Songthaew on the island — the fare depends on your destination beach; beaches further out cost more.

blocks.title: About boat times
blocks.html: Regular ferries tend to run in batches and wait for a reasonable number of passengers before leaving, while speedboats keep to clearer set times. If you reach Ban Phe in the late afternoon, check the time of the last boat first so you don't miss it.

blocks.text: How many days for Koh Samet

blocks.html: A day trip out in the morning and back in the evening is enough to swim at Sai Kaew, though it feels a little rushed and you'll miss the nighttime atmosphere. Most people go for 2 days and 1 night, which hits a nice balance: you get to swim, watch the sunset at Ao Phrao and stroll the beach in the evening. If you want to see several beaches without rushing, 3 days and 2 nights is the most relaxed, splitting it between a night on a lively beach and a night on a quiet one.

faq.q: Which Koh Samet beach is nicest, and who is it for?
faq.a: Sai Kaew is the biggest and liveliest, good for first-timers and families. Ao Wong Duean has shallow water that's easy for swimming plus full facilities. Ao Phrao is quiet and the place for sunsets, ideal for couples. Ao Thian and the southern beaches are quieter, good for anyone who wants a real rest.

faq.q: Which Koh Samet beach is best for the sunset?
faq.a: Ao Phrao is the only beach on the west side of the island, so it's where you can watch the sun set into the sea. East-side beaches like Sai Kaew, Wong Duean and Ao Thian are better for the sunrise in the morning, while Ao Kiu, on a narrow headland, lets you see both.

faq.q: What do you have to pay to visit Koh Samet?
faq.a: Mainly the boat from Ban Phe: a regular ferry is around ฿70/trip and a speedboat from around ฿200, plus the island (national park) entry fee, around ฿40 for Thais and ฿200 for foreigners, paid on arrival. Add a songthaew fare on the island if you're heading to a beach further out. Prices can change, so it's worth checking again on the spot.

faq.q: How many days should you spend on Koh Samet?
faq.a: A single day trip is enough for a swim but feels rushed. Most people favor 2 days and 1 night, which gets you both swimming and the sunset. If you want to take in several beaches at an easy pace, 3 days and 2 nights is just right.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Koh Samet?
faq.a: The dry season, roughly November to April, has the clearest sea and the calmest water, making it the best time to go. The rainy season is still doable but you may run into showers off and on and stronger waves, so check the forecast before you set off.
